blocks.text: A compressed-air receiver on a factory floor is a steel drum only a few millimetres thick holding air at 1 MPa or more. Its wall is thin enough that a simple free-body diagram gives the stresses exactly, and thin enough that when it fails the crack runs lengthwise along the shell, never around it. Why?

blocks.markdown: A vessel is **thin-walled** when the wall thickness $t$ (m) is small compared with the mean diameter $D$ (m), commonly $t/D\lesssim 1/20$. The wall then acts as a **membrane**: bending is negligible and the stress is taken as uniform through the thickness. We assume internal gauge pressure $p$ (Pa), closed ends, a circular cross-section, isotropic linear-elastic material and that $D$ is the mean diameter. Two normal stresses act in the wall: the **hoop** (circumferential) stress $\sigma_h$ and the **longitudinal** (axial) stress $\sigma_L$. The radial stress, varying from $-p$ at the inner surface to $0$ outside, is negligible compared with them.

blocks.title: Membrane stresses
blocks.text: Hoop stress $\sigma_h$ resists the pressure acting on a longitudinal cut through the cylinder. Longitudinal stress $\sigma_L$ resists the pressure acting on the closed end of a circumferential cut.

blocks.markdown: **Derivation sketch.** Cut a length $L$ of the cylinder along a diameter. The pressure force pushing the halves apart is $p\,D\,L$ (pressure times projected area). It is resisted by the wall cut at two places, each of area $tL$, so $pDL=2\sigma_h tL$ and $\sigma_h=pD/2t$. For the longitudinal stress cut across the cylinder: the pressure force on the end is $p\,\pi D^2/4$ and the wall area is $\pi D t$, so $\sigma_L=pD/4t$.

blocks.title: Stresses and diameter growth in an air receiver
blocks.prompt: A cylindrical steel air receiver has mean diameter $D=900$ mm, wall thickness $t=6$ mm and internal gauge pressure $p=1.2$ MPa. Use typical $E=200$ GPa and $\nu=0.30$. Find $\sigma_h$, $\sigma_L$ and the change in diameter.

steps.text: Longitudinal stress is half the hoop stress.
Hoop strain, with the longitudinal stress reducing it through the Poisson effect (radial stress neglected).
A circumferential strain equals the diametral strain, so the diameter change is the strain times $D$.
Longitudinal strain for reference: $\varepsilon_L=(\sigma_L-\nu\sigma_h)/E=9.000e-05$, so the length also grows slightly.

blocks.title: Minimum thickness of a spherical storage vessel
blocks.prompt: A spherical gas holder of mean diameter $D=3.0$ m stores gas at gauge pressure $p=1.5$ MPa. The allowable membrane stress is $\sigma_{allow}=120$ MPa (typical). Find the minimum wall thickness, and compare it with a cylinder of the same diameter, pressure and allowable stress.

steps.text: Sphere: every direction in the surface carries $pD/4t$. Set this equal to the allowable stress.
The sphere needs half the thickness of the cylinder, which is why large gas stores are spherical.

blocks.answer: Sphere $t_{min}=9.38$ mm; a cylinder would need 18.75 mm.

items: Use the **mean** diameter (inner diameter plus $t$) and pressures as **gauge** values.
Compute $\sigma_h$ first, then $\sigma_L=\sigma_h/2$ for a closed cylinder.
For design, divide by the allowable stress to get $t$; check $t/D$ is small enough for the thin-wall assumption.
For deformation, use the strain equations with both stresses and $\nu$; do not use $\varepsilon=\sigma/E$ alone.

blocks.title: Thin-wall limits
blocks.text: The formulas are accurate when $t/D\lesssim1/20$. For thicker walls the stress varies through the thickness (Lame theory) and the formulas under-predict the inner-surface stress.

blocks.title: Why seams split lengthwise
blocks.text: The hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress, so a boiler or sausage skin splits along its length first. A longitudinal weld seam must therefore be stronger than a circumferential one.

points: Thin sphere: $\sigma=pD/4t$ in every direction, so $t_{min}=pD/(4\sigma_{allow})$ is half that of a cylinder.
Diameter change uses biaxial Hooke's law: $\Delta D=D(\sigma_h-\nu\sigma_L)/E$ for a cylinder and $D(1-\nu)\sigma/E$ for a sphere.
The thin-wall results assume $t/D\lesssim1/20$ and a uniform stress through the thickness.

questions.stem: A closed cylindrical pressure vessel with a longitudinal weld seam and a circumferential weld seam is pressurised until it fails. Which statement best explains why a split along the longitudinal seam is more likely than one along the circumferential seam?

options.text: The hoop stress acting across the longitudinal seam is twice the longitudinal stress acting across the circumferential seam
The longitudinal stress is twice the hoop stress
Pressure acts only on the cylindrical surface, not the ends
Hoop and longitudinal stresses are equal in a closed cylinder

questions.correctOptionText: The hoop stress acting across the longitudinal seam is twice the longitudinal stress acting across the circumferential seam

distractorRationale.c: The end caps carry pressure and this load is what produces the longitudinal stress.
distractorRationale.d: Equal stresses occur in a sphere, not a cylinder.

questions.explanation: A longitudinal seam is loaded by the hoop stress, $pD/2t$, while a circumferential seam is loaded by the longitudinal stress, $pD/4t$. The hoop stress is double, so the longitudinal seam is the critical one.

questions.stem: A thin-walled closed cylinder has mean diameter 500 mm, wall thickness 4 mm and internal gauge pressure 0.8 MPa. Calculate the hoop stress in MPa.
questions.explanation: $\sigma_h=pD/2t=0.8\times500/(2\times4)=50$ MPa. Pressure in MPa and lengths in mm combine directly to give MPa.

questions.stem: A spherical pressure vessel has mean diameter 1.2 m and carries an internal gauge pressure of 2.4 MPa. The allowable membrane stress is 150 MPa (typical). What is the minimum wall thickness in mm?
questions.explanation: For a sphere $t=pD/(4\sigma_{allow})=2.4\times1200/(4\times150)=4.8$ mm. Using the cylinder formula by mistake would give 9.6 mm.

questions.stem: A thin cylinder and a thin sphere have the same mean diameter, the same wall thickness and carry the same internal pressure. How does the membrane stress in the sphere compare with the hoop stress in the cylinder?

distractorRationale.a: The sphere's stress equals the cylinder's longitudinal stress, not the hoop stress.
distractorRationale.d: $pD/8t$ does not appear in either case.

questions.explanation: The sphere carries $pD/4t$ in every direction, while the cylinder's hoop stress is $pD/2t$. The sphere is therefore twice as efficient in use of material.

questions.stem: A thin aluminium cylinder has mean diameter 400 mm, wall thickness 5 mm, and carries an internal gauge pressure of 1.6 MPa. Take $E=70$ GPa and $\nu=0.33$ (typical). Calculate the increase in diameter in mm. Assume closed ends and neglect radial stress.
questions.explanation: $\sigma_h=1.6\times400/10=64$ MPa and $\sigma_L=32$ MPa. The hoop strain is $(64-0.33\times32)/70000=7.634e-04$, so $\Delta D=400\times7.634e-04=0.305$ mm.

questions.stem: A cylindrical vessel with closed ends has mean diameter $D=800$ mm and carries 3.0 MPa gauge pressure. The allowable stress is 140 MPa (typical). Find the minimum wall thickness, state which stress governs, and explain why the other stress would permit a thinner wall.
markingGuide: The hoop stress is double the longitudinal stress, so it demands twice the thickness; the larger requirement governs.
Check $t/D=0.011$, which is within the thin-wall limit.
questions.explanation: Each stress component must stay below the allowable value, and the hoop stress is the larger one at $2\sigma_L$. So the design thickness comes from the hoop equation, 8.57 mm, and the axial requirement of 4.29 mm is satisfied automatically.

questions.stem: Derive the hoop stress in a thin-walled cylinder of mean diameter $D$ and wall thickness $t$ under internal pressure $p$ by considering a free body of the cylinder cut along a diameter. State the assumptions made.
markingGuide: Free body: a length $L$ of the cylinder cut along a diametral plane into two halves.
Pressure force on a half is $p\times D L$ (projected area), acting to separate the halves.
The wall is cut at two places, total area $2tL$, carrying $\sigma_h$.
Assumptions: thin wall ($t\ll D$), uniform stress through thickness, radial stress negligible, mean diameter used.
questions.explanation: The pressure acting on the inside of a half-cylinder has a net horizontal force equal to pressure times the projected rectangle $D\times L$. Two thin strips of wall resist it, giving the hoop stress formula directly.

questions.stem: A thin spherical shell has mean diameter 2.0 m, wall thickness 10 mm and carries 1.0 MPa gauge pressure. Take $E=200$ GPa and $\nu=0.30$ (typical). Calculate the increase in diameter in mm.
questions.explanation: The membrane stress is $pD/4t=1.0\times2000/40=50$ MPa in both directions, so the strain is $\varepsilon=(1-\nu)\sigma/E=0.7\times50/200000=1.750e-04$. Then $\Delta D=\varepsilon D=0.35$ mm.

questions.stem: A strain gauge reads the hoop strain on a thin steel cylinder ($\nu=0.30$) at the same point where another gauge reads the longitudinal strain. Assuming closed ends and neglecting radial stress, the ratio of hoop strain to longitudinal strain is

distractorRationale.a: This is the stress ratio, ignoring the Poisson effect on strains.
distractorRationale.b: This is the inverse stress ratio.
distractorRationale.d: Mixes the stress ratio with $1+\nu$, which does not arise.

questions.explanation: Taking $\sigma_L=\sigma_h/2$: $\varepsilon_h=(\sigma_h-\nu\sigma_h/2)/E=0.85\sigma_h/E$ and $\varepsilon_L=(\sigma_h/2-\nu\sigma_h)/E=0.20\sigma_h/E$. The ratio is $0.85/0.20=4.25$, much larger than the stress ratio of 2.

questions.stem: True or false: the thin-wall hoop stress formula $\sigma_h=pD/2t$ is derived by assuming the stress is uniform through the wall thickness.
questions.explanation: The membrane approximation takes $\sigma_h$ as constant across $t$, which is why $D$ is the mean diameter. When $t/D$ is no longer small, the stress varies through the wall and the thick-cylinder (Lame) equations must be used instead.
